source.title: Chat to chip: large language model based design of arbitrarily shaped metasurfaces
source.authors: Huanshu Zhang; Lei Kang; S. Campbell; D. Werner

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper and supplementary materials. It identifies itself as an accepted manuscript at Nanophotonics; the Version of Record may differ slightly.
record.tranche_reason: It benchmarks fine-tuned language models of different sizes on a downstream regression task and reports test-set errors, a different measure and setting from pretraining-loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study reports test-set MSEs for a fine-tuned optical-response prediction task across model sizes. These results bear on downstream performance versus scale, but it does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit scaling laws, test extrapolation from smaller runs, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. The architecture comparisons are not controlled at a fixed parameter count.
record.test_reason: It fine-tunes eleven open-weight LLMs (about 0.1B to 72B) on one metasurface spectrum-regression task and reports test MSE by size. That is a new downstream setting with a result bearing on V6. It fits no law, measures no pretraining loss and does not control architecture at fixed size, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. T3 fits better than T2: scaling is a side benchmark here, not the study's question.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right. The authors' main conclusion is that 1-D token-wise fine-tuned LLMs work as a practical forward and inverse design tool for arbitrarily shaped metasurfaces. On scale, they say accuracy trends upward with size but not monotonically, and that within-family size changes give only modest shifts. They add that Gemma offers the best accuracy-to-cost ratio and that future gains are likelier from stronger numerical priors or VLMs than from parameter scaling alone.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes open-weight LLMs for metasurface spectrum regression and benchmarks test-set MSE. It does not use the original studies' held-out language-model pretraining loss measurements or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The benchmark reports non-monotonic accuracy across model sizes and says architecture can outweigh parameter count; it also reports diminishing MSE returns with Qwen-2.5 scaling from 7B to 72B. Fine-tuning epoch sensitivity is reported for Llama-3.1-8B, but does not test a claim version about scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Model family (Gemma ranks first or second in every size band, plausibly because of its digit-friendly tokenizer) and reasoning-tuned priors affect accuracy more than parameter count. Several reasoning models failed to produce the numeric output format at all.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For fine-tuned numerical regression, model family, tokenizer and instruction priors can outweigh parameter count.

record.problems: The evidence concerns one optical-response task and one train-test split, not language-model pretraining loss or a broad range of downstream tasks. The text gives only selected benchmark MSEs; other values are in Figure 3, whose plotted data are not provided numerically in the supplied text. There is no controlled architecture comparison at a fixed parameter count and no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional benchmark-model rows were extracted from Figure 3 because their numerical values are not stated in the supplied text. The DNN comparisons, Llama epoch sweep, and inverse-design results do not measure scale-related downstream predictability for V6.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating from fits on small runs.
Shape comparisons at fixed parameter count; the authors state no deeper architectural tests were done.
Power-law form under fine-tuning or other regimes; no law is fitted.
Whether gains follow a predictable (fitted) curve, the link to pretraining loss, and tasks beyond this single regression task.

missing.what: Per-model test MSE for all eleven benchmarked LLMs across the three size bands (plotted only)
Authors' summary that changing model size within an LLM family produces only modest accuracy shifts, versus a larger spread for DNNs

record.verdict_notes: This is weak evidence for V6: one task, one split, no uncertainty estimates, mostly cross-family comparisons, and most values available only in a figure. The study cites Kaplan et al. only to justify reusing the mid-size fine-tuning configuration for other model sizes.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Predicting much larger runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute and their trends with compute.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, and other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Whether a power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes; fine-tuning is used, but no power law is tested.
The study tests fine-tuned optical-response regression across model sizes, not a range of downstream tasks or the relation to pretraining loss.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or dependence of scaling laws on fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Moving from tiny (0.1B) to small/mid-size models on fine-tuned spectrum regression
relationships.reason: MSE falls from >14.7e-3 (SmolLM2-0.1B) to 3.4e-3 (Gemma-2-3B), and accuracy generally improves with size (r1, r5).
relationships.display_finding: Mean squared error falls from above 14.7e-3 for SmolLM2-0.1B to 3.4e-3 for Gemma-2-3B, with accuracy generally improving as model size increases.

relationships.condition: Across model families in the 7–9B band, and same-family scaling beyond 7B
relationships.reason: Gains are not monotonic across families (Mistral 7B beats Llama 8B), and Qwen-2.5 7B to 72B cuts MSE by only 1.2e-3, which the authors call diminishing returns (r1, r6).
relationships.display_finding: Mistral 7B outperformed Llama 8B, while increasing Qwen-2.5 from 7B to 72B reduced MSE by only 1.2e-3.

reader_labels.reason: The authors report that accuracy generally improves with increasing size; this supports a broad scale-performance trend in the tested task (r1).
